prompts.flavor: The hollow hills are still occupied. The tenants keep a different count of years.
prompts.rules: Any god, hero or creature from the myths and folklore of Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Cornwall, Man and Brittany, or of the ancient Britons and Gauls, by any spelling. Arthur's Welsh tales count; saints, figures from the history books and French additions to Arthur don't.

prompts.text: Name a creature or spirit of Japanese folklore.
prompts.flavor: A hundred candles, a hundred stories. Blow out the last one and see who is still sitting with you.
prompts.rules: Any yokai, ghost, demon, beast or spirit of Japanese folklore and legend, Okinawan and Ainu ones included, by any romanisation, and the kami of Shinto myth too. Creatures made up for modern manga, anime, films and games don't count.

answers.lore: A fox grows another tail every hundred years, some say, until it has nine.

A two-faced, four-armed being of Hida in the Nihon Shoki of 720, nearly 1,300 years before Jujutsu Kaisen borrowed him.
King of the underworld and judge of the dead. Japanese children are warned that he keeps a special punishment for liars.
A scaly sea creature who, in a print of 1846, said a picture of it would ward off plague. In 2020 Japan's health ministry used it again.

prompts.text: Name a god of the Aztecs, the Maya or the Inca.
prompts.flavor: Four suns have come and gone, the Aztecs said. This is the fifth, and there will not be a sixth.
prompts.rules: Any god or goddess of the Aztecs and other Nahua peoples, the Maya, or the Inca and their Andean neighbours, by any spelling, the divine heroes of their myths included. Kings, conquerors and creatures of later folklore don't count.

prompts.text: Name a god, hero or monster of ancient Mesopotamia.
prompts.flavor: They were written in clay before anyone wrote anything else. Clay keeps. So, it seems, do they.

answers.lore: Hero of the oldest great story we know. A tablet of his epic, looted from Iraq in 1991, was sent home from the United States in 2021.

Became king of the gods by defeating Tiamat, then made heaven and earth out of the two halves of her.

He warned one man of the coming flood, getting round his oath to the other gods by whispering it to the wall of his reed hut.

Marduk's snake-dragon, striding across the Ishtar Gate in glazed brick. Early excavators misread its name as 'sirrush'.
A lion-headed eagle that stole the Tablet of Destinies from Enlil, and with it the power to rule the universe.
A scorpion man and his wife guard the gate of the mountains where the sun rises and sets.
The wise alewife at the edge of the world, who told Gilgamesh to enjoy good food, dancing and the people he loved.
A sage who turned down the bread and water of eternal life, because his patron Ea had warned him they would kill him.
A king who flew up to heaven on an eagle's back, looking for the plant of birth so that he could have a son.

Gatekeeper of the underworld, who made Inanna give up a jewel or a garment at each of its seven gates.
The winter god. In a Sumerian debate poem he argued with his brother Emesh, summer, over who was the better farmer, and won.
